BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Saturday, a closed low with an elongated southern trough begins to swing up and north of the forecast area, bringing the trough, a cold front, and wetter conditions.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry through Thursday, with near normal temperatures.
- Precipitation chances increasing across higher terrain Friday afternoon. Becoming widespread Saturday afternoon into Sunday.
- A drying and warming trend will set in Monday, through at least midweek.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Following the departing shortwave, skies have continued to clear across southeast Oregon and southwest Idaho. With light winds and mostly clear skies tonight, radiational cooling will allow temperatures to drop into the upper 20s to mid 30s across many lower valleys,resulting in areas of patchy frost late tonight into Thursday morning.

A brief warming and drying trend will take hold on Thursday as weak transient ridging moves overhead ahead of an approaching upper level developing off the Pacific Northwest coast. Afternoon temperatures on Thursday will rebound to near or slightly above seasonal, with quiet weather prevailing across the region through early Thursday evening.

Late Thursday night into early Friday, southwesterly flow aloft will strengthen over the Great Basin and northern Intermountain West.A weak shortwave trough embedded in this southwesterly flow will lift northeastward across the area. While moisture availability remains somewhat limited, sufficient moisture will advect northward to south-central Idaho to support isolated to scattered showers late Thursday night through Friday.

Snow levels will hover around 6000 to 7000 feet during morning increasing to 8000 feet by afternoon. This will primarily yield light rain in the lower valleys, but a dusting to a few inches of snow possible across the higher peaks and mountain passes, including Banner Summit. For the remainder of southwest Idaho and southeast Oregon, Friday will feature passing cloud cover and slightly cooler afternoon temperatures, with dry conditions continuing through Friday night before the main Pacific trough approaches for the weekend.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Saturday, a closed low with an elongated southern trough begins to swing up and north of the forecast area, bringing the trough, a cold front, and wetter conditions. This trough will have a good pull of Pacific moisture ahead of it, with precipitable water values increasing to around the 90th percentile in southwest Idaho. The anomalous atmospheric moisture will be coincident with largescale forcing, leading to increasing precipitation chances through the day Saturday, reaching 50-80% Saturday evening and night as a cold front crosses the area. Hopefully your plan is to dress up as Mary Poppins for Halloween, just in case. Snow levels will initially begin at 6-8 kft MSL, lowering to 4.5-6.5 kft MSL by Sunday afternoon. Lowering snow levels occur alongside decreasing precipitation chances as conditions dry out behind the front. Overall, the bulk of any snow accumulation will remain above 6.5 kft MSL, with generally 2-5 inches of accumulation (Locally up to 7 on the highest peaks). The lowering snow levels could allow for snow or wintry mix as low as 4.5 kft Sunday, although little accumulation is anticipated as precipitation tapers off behind the departing system. Ridging will build in behind the departing system, allowing for dry conditions Monday afternoon through at least mid-week. Temperatures will be seasonable or below normal throughout the period.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Models are showing very strong winds behind the front, with speeds around 40kts to 70kts at 700mb on the back side of the low.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mild and mostly dry through the work week.
- Unsettled weather returns late this weekend and early next week. Mountain snow is likely (>70% chance) above 8500ft during this time. High uncertainty remains for the foothills and plains.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A weak front is currently moving south through our forecast area as of 12:45pm. Behind the front, winds have turned more northerly, with gusts around 15 to 25mph. Overall the impact of the front will be limited, with the exception of the brief wind shift today. Light winds and mostly clear skies could allow for another morning of low clouds and fog for the eastern plains. Weak downsloping and lower moisture will likely prevent fog from developing in the urban corridor, but we could see some patchy fog with visiblities below 1 mile further east/northeast. Any low clouds and fog that developed overnight will dissipate by the mid to late morning. Moisture will increase at upper levels (300mb) on Thursday, leading to an increase in high cloud cover for the afternoon. High temperatures will be a few degrees cooler tomorrow for much of the plains, compared to today.

Remnants from Tropical Storm Vance are forecast to be absorbed into the southwest flow aloft, moving through West Texas Thursday and Friday towards eastern CO and Kansas for late Friday. Right now, models have the bulk of the moisture moving to our east. But, a weak shortwave could still produce enough lift for some light rain showers across the far eastern plains late Friday. On Saturday, another shortwave is forecast to move over the area. But this activity should primarily be confined to the mountains, where moisture will be more prevalent.

There is still a lot of uncertainty with the system late Sunday into early next week. Here are a few things we do know with this system: a strong upper trough/low will move near or over the area sometime late Sunday into early Tuesday, a strong cold front will move through at some point late Sunday into late Monday, and this system will bring strong lift and increased precipitation chances for at least portions of the area. The things that are still very uncertain this far out and will have significant influence on the potential impacts in our area: the track of the upper level low and development of the surface low (aka the exact direction of the winds/potential for upslope and area of highest forcing), the surface temperatures behind the front which will have impacts on precip type, how the subtropical jet and trough will interact with the deep trough moving out of the Northwest, and if moisture will be able to wrap around the low as it moves east of the area.

Models are showing very strong winds behind the front, with speeds around 40kts to 70kts at 700mb on the back side of the low. If the low ends up tracking in a way where there's a more easterly component to these strong winds, precipitation chances and amounts in the foothills and adjacent plains would look much more promising. Right now, the best chance for precipitation and snow will be in the higher terrain with snow levels starting the event around 10kft to 11kft and gradually dropping closer to 6,500 to 7,000ft by Tuesday morning. Snow chances for areas below 7,000 ft remain low (<15%) at this time. However, this is something we'll need to keep a close eye on as we get closer to the event. Finally, with the strong winds and much colder conditions behind the front, there is potential for wind chills in the upper teens across portions of the plains Tuesday morning.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Regardless of the precipitation outcome, a cold front will sweep through the area Sunday night, bringing colder and windier conditions into the area for Monday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry, warm, and breezy conditions are expected to continue through Thursday, with mild overnight lows.
- Chances for a few showers return Saturday (Halloween) with temperatures remaining mild.
- A pattern change to colder, wetter, and windier conditions is favored Sunday into Tuesday, but the details remain highly uncertain at this time.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The shortwave ending up sagging further south than what model guidance was showing yesterday. The cloud cover and showers were slated for Central and Northern portions of Wyoming. The showers ended up cutting right through Southeast Wyoming with thick low level clouds covering the Nebraska Panhandle. Most of the precipitation from these showers ended up being virga so little to no rainfall actually reached the surface. Besides possible fog come Friday morning... the forecast really hasn't changed. 700mb temperatures are really stable around 6C and the upper level ridge is still the dominant weather regime for the next 48 hours. Daily high temperatures are going to remain in the 60's Thursday and Friday with overnight temperatures in the 30's and 40's for a pretty average fall-like couple of days. The vorticity and Warm/Cold air advection are pretty standard and nothing to write home about. So the ridge is really just performing how it should and suppressing any convection over the next couple days.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Most of the area will see pleasant conditions for Halloween trick-or- treating this year. Broad ridging will remain over the area this weekend, supporting above average high temperatures ranging from the upper 50s in Carbon and Albany counties to the low to mid 60s over the High Plains. Expect a mix of cloud cover and sunshine as plentiful moisture moves over the area aloft. A weak vort-max passing through the area in the southwest flow overhead will help to support a few afternoon and evening showers, mainly over and near the higher terrain, but the chance for appreciable rainfall or thunder is low. Due to high humidity and cloud cover, overnight low temperatures will be mild for this time of year, only dropping to the upper 30s to lower 40s east of I-25, and mid to upper 30s to the west. Near saturated conditions will produce the potential for some spooky fog to develop both Saturday morning and Saturday night. Sunday looks mild again, but slightly cooler than Saturday with skies becoming mostly cloudy ahead of the next storm system approaching the area.

A complex storm system will push across the western CONUS Sunday into early next week. Two major players will make up this system: first, a strong, moisture-laden upper level low riding the subtropical jet stream into the southwest and second, a potent Pacific trough pushing into the northwest. The primary questions concerning the evolution of this system are if, when, and where the two approaching systems might merge together. Ensembles have shifted slightly over the last 24 hours, but have yet to converge on a solution. Thus, several scenarios still remain, though the probabilities have changed. In the first scenario (approx 40% chance), the two features do not merge at all. Two separate mid- level circulations competing with one other would mean muddy forcing forcing for ascent and limited precipitation potential. We could still expect some rain and snow showers, but amounts would be modest (0.25" or less for Laramie, Cheyenne, Wheatland, Scottsbluff, 0.25" to 0.5" in Rawlins and Chadron). In the second scenario (approx 50% chance), the two systems merge, but this occurs a little too late and a little too far east for a widespread major precipitation event for our area. Still, it would be enough for a moderate rain event over western Nebraska, and some potential for accumulating snow especially for the elevated ridges (Cheyenne Ridge & Pine Ridge). The scenario in which the two systems merge early enough to produce a major event has decreased in probability (to around 10%) as fewer ensembles now show this potential. The ECMWF Extreme Forecast Index for QPF today has decreased slightly as well to around 0.5 to 0.6 over much of the area. This tells us that while an anomalous event is still possible, only a small subset of ensemble members show this, keeping confidence low.

Overall probabilities for 0.5" of liquid precipitation are the lowest around Laramie, Cheyenne, and Wheatland (30-40%). Probabilities increase both east and west, with Rawlins around a 50% chance to exceed 0.5" and the Sidney to Chadron corridor in the 60 to 70% range. In addition to the uncertainty in QPF, there is also uncertainty in the snow levels with very marginal temperatures for snow over much of the area. Cooler air moving in through the event should lead to snow levels starting fairly high (perhaps 9000 ft) and then dropping overnight Sunday night and through the day Monday. The question is how low they can get. Thus, there is fairly good confidence in accumulating snow for the mountains (90+% chance for 1" and 50% chance for 6"), but lower confidence around where most folks live. The best chances for 1" or more of snow outside of the mountains are in the valleys of Carbon and Albany counties, and the elevated ridges of the High Plains.

Regardless of the precipitation outcome, a cold front will sweep through the area Sunday night, bringing colder and windier conditions into the area for Monday. Which of the above scenarios that ends up playing out will also affect the wind direction and potential for high winds. Still, there is high confidence in a windy day along and east of the Laramie range. About 25% of ensemble members have 700-mb winds sufficiently high to support widespread high wind potential, while the I-80 summit area has about a 50% chance for high winds. Look for lingering impacts in the form of cool temperatures and windy conditions on Tuesday, but we should start to lose the wind and warm up slightly by Wednesday.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Colder, drier air continues to invade Monday night and early Tuesday. Precipitation will taper off significantly Monday afternoon, but the shoulders of the western Divide will hang on to some light snow and rain into Tuesday morning.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mild fall conditions continue through tomorrow.
- Increasing precipitation chances arrive Friday morning with light rain and snow above 10000 feet.
- Deeper moisture arrives Saturday night and will increase the chances for impactful precipitation for southwest CO Sunday and Monday.
- River flooding seems unlikely, but localized impacts due to rainfall on saturated soils are expected.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Mild fall conditions continue across the West Slope through Thursday. A shift in the synoptic pattern begins to take shape Thursday afternoon as low pressure drops into the PACNW. This will send a southwesterly fetch of Pacific moisture into the Southwest. High based cloud cover will begin to blanket the region, while the low levels of the atmosphere stay dry into Friday. By Friday morning some weak orographic showers are possible for southeast UT and southwest CO. The scarcity of moisture at this point will keep accumulations near trace values. Moisture continues to increase Friday and Saturday, with light rain and snow possible through Saturday. Snow levels remain above 10000 feet with daytime temperatures keeping any accumulations in check. Below snow line, rainfall is expected to remain on the light side. However, a few isolated thunderstorms remain in the forecast. This could produce heavier showers on Friday and Saturday afternoon.

By Sunday, AR(atmospheric river) moisture begins to fill in across the Southwest. The trajectory of this plume still favors a more southerly track, keeping our CWA out of some of the heaviest rainfall potential. However, ensemble models continue to highlight an area of 1 to 2 inches of rainfall potential over southwest CO. On the heels of heavy rainfall last weekend, this is expected to have some adverse effects on runoff near saturated hillsides. River flooding continues to look unlikely at these values spread over 48 hours. However, localized impacts from mud, rocks, and debris flows on saturated hillsides are likely. These impacts will seem more pronounced in areas still cleaning up last week's mess. Rainfall begins to peak early Monday morning as the frontal boundary swings through. This will drop snow levels to around 8000 feet overnight and Monday morning. Mountain passes will likely see some travel slowdowns for motorists Monday morning and into the afternoon, as snow levels drop more behind the front. Afternoon highs on Monday will struggle to reach the 50s for many of our low valleys.

Colder, drier air continues to invade Monday night and early Tuesday. Precipitation will taper off significantly Monday afternoon, but the shoulders of the western Divide will hang on to some light snow and rain into Tuesday morning. Light orographic rain and snow continues on the terrain Wednesday, with minimal additional accumulation.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Either way, the deepening trough out west will likely bring accumulating snow to the mountains this weekend. Showers will start more isolated in nature, increasing in coverage later in the weekend and into early next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Drier and warmer through Thursday, with a pattern shift starting on Friday.
- Low to medium chance for locally dense fog over the eastern plains late tonight into Thursday morning.
- Potential for mountain snows and heavy rain along with the additional flooding returns over the Continental Divide and the San Luis Valley Sunday into Monday.
- Mountains snows increase Monday, with a low chance for at least a wintry mix over portions of the mountain valleys and plains.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Relatively quiet weather will persist this period as a drier air mass and westerly flow remain in place, and as rising heights are expected through the period. Will keep a close eye on fog potential over the far eastern plains late tonight into early Thursday morning, along with isolated thunderstorm development over the far southeast plains late Thursday afternoon.

Currently, a cold front has pushed south down the plains and is moving into the northeast CWA. Meanwhile, surface trough is situated right along the Colorado, Kansas, and Oklahoma boundaries. The cold front is worth monitoring as higher dewpoint air along this boundary could help with redeveloping fog late tonight, which actually occurred along and ahead of this boundary to the north earlier this morning. Did add areas of fog to forecast, but there is a low to medium chance for locally dense fog. The trough will be worth monitoring as this focus along with increased moisture could serve to help develop at least isolated thunderstorm development late Thursday afternoon. Confidence is low, but with some pieces of guidance hinting at this possibility.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Calm and mild conditions will continue on Thursday, though temperatures will drop a few degrees thanks to a dry cold front passing through.

Starting on Friday, our next incoming source of moisture will be a deepening trough over the Pacific northwest. As we move into this weekend, southwest flow aloft will increase over the region, bringing in moist Pacific air and better forcing to western Colorado. Meanwhile, deterministic guidance suggests a shortwave passing south of our area during the day on Friday, which could potentially bring some rain to the far southeast plains as well. However, if the wave picks up in speed, most of the precipitation could miss us, falling in Kansas instead.

Either way, the deepening trough out west will likely bring accumulating snow to the mountains this weekend. Showers will start more isolated in nature, increasing in coverage later in the weekend and into early next week. Latest guidance shows the upper trough amplifying, with a secondary low potentially moving onshore from the southwest as the trough digs into the Four Corners. Details on the timing, strength, and path of the system still need to be refined in the data, but overall cooler and more active weather is currently expected for next week.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Precipitation looks to taper off through Monday morning, with drier conditions prevailing through the remainder of the day. Low temperatures will be some of the coolest of the season so far early next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry and seasonably cool conditions continue through Thursday.

- An influx of tropical moisture brings scattered showers and thunderstorms on Friday, with potential to produce locally heavy rainfall leading to an increased flash flood threat mainly across southwest and west-central Utah.
- A stronger system taps into deep moisture from an atmospheric river on Sunday, producing widespread light to moderate, locally heavy rainfall across the region.
- A cooler airmass moves in late Sunday, with snow levels dropping to 7000 feet early Monday morning, allowing for substantial high elevation mountain snow accumulation.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Dry, southwesterly flow across the region prevails through Thursday on the leading edge of a longwave trough currently situated off the west coast. This will keep dry and seasonably cool conditions in place through this period.

A shift in the pattern is expected on Friday as moist, southerly flow strengthens across the region as a northern stream low pressure system begins to phase into a tropical low off the Baja Peninsula. Concurrently, a shortwave trough ejecting northeastward on the eastern periphery of the parent trough will traverse our region through the day, introducing more substantial instability especially across southwest and west- central Utah on Friday afternoon. The combination of this tropical moisture influx with increasing instability will allow scattered showers and thunderstorms to develop by late Friday morning through the evening, with the main threat for heavy rainfall and resultant flash flooding focused where instability is maximized across southwest and west-central Utah. There is a considerable forecast bust scenario that still exists in models, as around 33% of members suggest the northern stream trough remaining decoupled from the tropical low, which would keep dry, southwesterly flow in place through this period. This lower end scenario would essentially squash the flash flood risk on Friday, so keep an eye on the forecast as we continue to monitor this potential.

A brief period of subsidence is expected behind the exiting shortwave on Saturday, with shower activity gradually tapering off Sunday morning. A relative lull is expected through the day, but will be brief as our next, likely wetter, system begins to move into the region. The northern stream trough and tropical low are expected to shift inland late Saturday. This will transport more substantial amounts of moisture into the region given the tropical low tapping into a strong atmospheric river, allowing widespread precipitation to begin filling in from the south as early as late Saturday. Models have started to converge on northern Utah tapping into more considerable precipitation, mainly due to a strong cold front passage as the northern stream trough digs into the Great Basin on Sunday. With northwesterly flow developing behind the front and much colder temperatures aloft, potential for lake enhanced precipitation will also come into the mix late Sunday into Monday morning. While widespread heavy precipitation is likely late Saturday through Monday morning, there still is a notable spread in potential accumulation amounts. For most areas, the 25th percentile indicates widespread totals in the 0.2-0.5" range, while the 75th percentile indicates totals between 0.75-1.25". For southwest Utah, the Wasatch Front, and all Utah mountains, higher totals are favored across the percentile ranges, with the 25th percentile indicating accumulations between 0.5-1", and 75th percentile between 1.5-2.5".

Behind the cold front late Sunday, snow levels are expected to drop as low as 6500-7000 feet by early Monday morning. With lingering showers expected to continue through this period, especially downstream of the GSL from lake enhancement, precipitation is expected to transition to snow and bring notable accumulations especially to areas above 8000 feet. Current forecast shows generally 3-6 inches above 8000 feet, with higher totals between 8-14 inches above 9000 feet.

Precipitation looks to taper off through Monday morning, with drier conditions prevailing through the remainder of the day. Low temperatures will be some of the coolest of the season so far early next week.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Heavy rain on Wednesday and Thursday triggered small wet avalanches in the west-Central and Southern Mountains, but this concern is waning as temperatures drop. The most likely place to trigger an avalanche is at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) in the Southern and west-Central Mountains on west, north, and east-facing slopes where new snow has been accumulating and a layer of mid-October snow persists. The Northern Mountains remain mostly bare.

This weekend, a new storm will deliver 4 to 8 inches of snow to the San Juan and Sangre de Cristo Mountains, creating fresh avalanche concerns on upper-elevation, wind-drifted slopes facing west, north, and east. Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

(Precipitation data are recorded from Secesh SNOTEL site at 6540')
